subject: Civil Engineering
title: Bus Rapid Transit: Buses That Act Like Trains
description: A fast breakdown of Bus Rapid Transit: Buses That Act Like Trains for builders.

hook.text: Curitiba, Brazil, built a metro system using buses — at a fraction of the cost.

buildup.text: BRT uses dedicated lanes, level boarding, and off-board fare collection — like rail.

discovery.text: Articulated buses carry 160 passengers. Bi-articulated ones carry 270 — train capacity.

twist.text: BRT can be built in two years. A metro line takes ten or more — time matters.

climax.text: Bogotá's TransMilenio moves 2.4 million daily — the world's busiest BRT system.

punchline.text: Give buses their own lane and they become a metro on rubber tires.

quiz.question: What makes BRT different from a regular bus service?
options: BRT uses smaller vehicles for faster acceleration
BRT has dedicated lanes, level boarding, and operates like a rail system
BRT runs only during off-peak hours to reduce congestion

details.summary: Bus rapid transit (BRT) provides rail-like service using buses on dedicated lanes with level boarding, off-board fare collection, and signal priority at intersections.
details.whyItMatters: BRT democratizes high-quality public transit by delivering metro-like performance at 10-30% of rail construction costs. Bogotá's TransMilenio proved BRT could move 45,000 passengers per hour per direction.
takeaways: Dedicated bus lanes ensure BRT operates independently of traffic congestion
Level boarding and off-board fare collection eliminate dwell time delays
BRT systems cost $5-30 million per kilometer versus $100-500 million for metro

faq.question: What features distinguish BRT from a regular bus route?
faq.answer: BRT requires physically separated lanes preventing car intrusion, enclosed stations with platform-level boarding, pre-paid fare collection before boarding, GPS-based signal priority at intersections, and frequent all-day service.

faq.question: Can BRT really match rail transit performance?
faq.answer: Top BRT systems like Bogotá's TransMilenio carry passenger volumes comparable to many metro lines. However, the highest-capacity metro systems still exceed BRT capacity.
